query: Design a lightweight alloy (<6 g/cm³) containing Magnesium and transition metals, constrained by the need to limit sintering temperature between 800 °C and 1000 °C to balance relative density and elemental volatility. The material currently suffers from unstable microstructures and poor functional properties (oxidation/corrosion) due to unclear phase transformation pathways and element segregation. Request a hypothesis on how to navigate this temperature window to form a dense, single-phase-like microstructure that maximizes barrier properties. Include prior evidence on the limitations of standard sintering in this regime, define the boundary where density fails or volatility occurs, and propose a falsification experiment comparing intermediate temperatures against the proposed optimum.

generation.hypothesis: A Mg-based lightweight alloy (<6 g/cm³) containing transition metals (e.g., Ti, Zr, Mn) can achieve a dense, single-phase-like microstructure with superior oxidation/corrosion barrier properties by utilizing a narrow sintering window (850–900 °C) combined with rapid thermal cycling to suppress element segregation and volatile loss, while promoting sluggish diffusion-driven solid solution formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder mixture of Mg (lightweight base) and transition metals (Ti, Zr, Mn) with high surface area, prone to segregation and volatile loss during standard sintering.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled sintering protocol at 850–900 °C (within the 800–1000 °C constraint) using rapid heating/cooling cycles to minimize dwell time at peak temperature, thereby balancing densification kinetics against elemental volatility and phase instability.
generation.conditions: Sintering temperature: 850–900 °C; Atmosphere: Inert (Ar) to prevent oxidation during processing; Heating rate: >50 °C/min; Cooling rate: >100 °C/min; Pressure: Optional spark plasma sintering (SPS) to enhance densification at lower temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Sluggish diffusion kinetics induced by multi-component transition metal addition, which stabilizes a single-phase solid solution and suppresses topologically-close-packed (TCP) phase formation, while rapid thermal cycling prevents grain coarsening and element segregation.
generation.mechanism: The narrow temperature window (850–900 °C) avoids the volatility threshold of Mg (>900 °C) while providing sufficient thermal energy for diffusion-driven homogenization. Rapid thermal cycling limits the time available for phase separation and volatile loss, promoting a metastable single-phase-like microstructure that enhances barrier properties against oxidation/corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative density >95% with minimal porosity, single-phase-like microstructure (FCC/BCC solid solution), and significantly improved oxidation/corrosion resistance due to a uniform, protective surface oxide layer (e.g., MgO/TiO2/ZrO2 composite).
generation.baseline: Standard sintering at 950–1000 °C leads to Mg volatility, element segregation, and multi-phase microstructures with poor barrier properties and reduced density due to pore formation.
generation.boundary: Density fails (<90%) if sintering temperature <800 °C due to insufficient diffusion; Volatility dominates (>5% Mg loss) if temperature >950 °C, leading to porosity and microstructural instability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal temperature window may vary based on specific transition metal ratios and powder morphology; long-term thermal stability of the single-phase structure at service temperatures >800 °C requires further validation.
generation.falsification_experiment: Compare sintered samples at 800 °C, 850 °C, 900 °C, 950 °C, and 1000 °C using identical powder mixtures. Measure relative density (Archimedes method), phase composition (XRD), microstructure (SEM/EBSD), and oxidation/corrosion resistance (weight gain in 5% NaCl solution at 60 °C). Hypothesis is falsified if the 850–900 °C samples do not show superior density (>95%) and barrier properties compared to other temperatures, or if volatility losses exceed 5% at 900 °C.

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
